note:
Amos introduces himself and his prophecy, specifying the time when God’s word came to him.

**The words of Amos.** The prophet’s messages are introduced with this formula (cf. Jer. 1:1). Amos is God’s covenant lawsuit messenger, bringing God’s suit against disobedient Israel.

**shepherds.** The Hb. term probably refers to keepers of a particular kind of sheep known for its unusually fine wool. The king of Moab is noted as owning such sheep (2 Kin. 3:4).

**Tekoa.** This village was five miles (8 km) south of Bethlehem. Because of its good pastureland, it supported many shepherds with their flocks.

**the earthquake.** Since this earthquake was remembered in a region prone to seismic activity, it must have been of considerable magnitude, and it would have acted as a reminder of divine judgment, as in Zech. 14:5.

LORD. See note on Ex. 3:15.

**roars.** As a shepherd, Amos knows well the terrifying roar of a lion on the attack (1 Sam. 17:34–37). The Lord Himself roars from Zion to announce His judgment (Jer. 25:30; Joel 3:16). These opening words of judgment set the tone for what follows.

**pastures ... withers.** The Lord’s judgment will affect the whole land, from the pastures to the forested top of Carmel, rich in orchards and vineyards (Lev. 26:19; Deut. 28:23, 24).

This series of prophecies begins with six Gentile nations: Syria, Philistia, Phoenicia, Edom, Ammon, and Moab. Some of the transgressions mentioned here have nothing to do with Israel or Judah. The sins listed are crimes against humanity and therefore God Himself. After addressing the sins of the Gentile nations, the oracles dramatically turn against Judah (2:4, 5) and Israel (2:6–16).

**1:3 For three transgressions ... for four.** This refrain, repeated with each prophecy, is an example of parallelism using ascending numbers for emphasis (cf. Ps. 62:11; Mic. 5:5). This standard device in ancient Near Eastern poetry is not intended to be taken literally, but means “for many transgressions.”

**Damascus.** David defeated and garrisoned this royal city of Syria (2 Sam. 8:6). During Solomon’s reign Damascus broke free, with Rezon as king (1 Kin. 11:23–25).

**sledges of iron.** The threshing sledge was a wooden board with teeth of iron or basalt fixed on the underside. An ox would pull the sledge over the grain while the driver stood on it. This symbol portrays how the Syrians treated Gilead with extreme cruelty (2 Kin. 13:7).

This refrain (1:7, 10, 12, 14; 2:2, 5) in each of the messages is also found in Hosea (8:14) and Jeremiah (17:27; 21:14; 50:32). Fire was widely understood in the ancient Near East to be an instrument of divine judgment. It was often used in warfare, and was considered one way that a god purged a rebellious people. This pagan understanding also reflects a truth revealed in Scripture: the true God will in fact judge by fire (2 Pet. 3:7 note).

**Hazael.** The king of Syria (c. 841–801 B.C.), whose reign was predicted by the prophet Elisha (2 Kin. 8:13).

**strongholds.** Fortified citadel-palaces of the nobility.

**Ben-hadad.** A throne name, like “Pharaoh” in Egypt. Probably the third king with this name is meant. The first assisted Judah’s king Asa against Israel’s Baasha (1 Kin. 15:18–20). The second, Ben-hadad II, was assassinated by the usurper Hazael (2 Kin. 8:14, 15). Hazael’s son, Ben-hadad III, was contemporary with Jehoahaz of Israel (2 Kin. 13:25). It was he who made Israel’s army “like the dust at threshing” (2 Kin. 13:7).

The verb is often used to indicate annihilation by war (Josh. 23:4; Is. 10:7).

**the inhabitants.** The Hb. term is lit. “the one who sits,” possibly a reference to the king rather than the whole population. The same word is used of God sitting or enthroned as king in Pss. 2:4; 22:3 (“enthroned”); 29:10.

**Valley of Aven.** Lit. “Valley of Wickedness.” Possibly it refers to ancient Syrian Heliopolis, now called Baalbek, in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon. It was apparently a center for sun worship. The phrase itself may be an indirect reference to a pagan deity.

**Beth-eden.** Probably a district about two hundred miles (320 km) northeast of Damascus (not to be confused with the Garden of Eden; cf. Gen. 2:8 note), and ruled by a Syrian vassal king. The point of the parallelism between the Valley of Aven and Beth-eden is to indicate that not only Damascus, but its territories as well, will be undone.

**Syria ... to Kir.** The original home of the Syrians (9:7), Kir will become their place of exile.

The southernmost of the five Philistine royal cities, which are Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath, and Gaza. Located between Egypt and Canaan, Gaza was a natural center for trade.

**whole people.** That is, an entire group of exiles (also v. 9). The Philistine trade included slaves. Prisoners of war usually became slaves, but here a whole population was sold into slavery. The apparent reference is to the capture and sale of Israelites during the reign of Jehoram (2 Chr. 21:16, 17).

**to Edom.** Edom is an alternative name for Esau, the brother of Jacob/Israel (Gen. 25:30). Although originally closely related to the Israelites, the Edomites received Israelites as slaves from the Philistines. For its role in the Edomites’ sin against their brother Israelites, Gaza, which stands for Philistia as a whole, is now sentenced.

A strong and prosperous Philistine capital city located eighteen miles (29 km) northeast of Gaza.

**Ashkelon.** The third royal city, located halfway between Gaza and Ashdod on the Mediterranean coast.

**Ekron.** The fourth royal city of the Philistines, located on the border of the territories allotted to Judah and Dan (Josh. 15:11, 45, 46; 19:43. Gath, the fifth royal city, is not mentioned because it had already been defeated by Hazael at the time Amos wrote (2 Kin. 12:17). Assyria was the primary instrument of judgment against all these cities, and all four are subsequently mentioned in Assyrian annals as vassals of Esarhaddon (681–669 B.C.) and Ashurbanipal (668–627 B.C.).

One of two major Phoenician cities (the other is Sidon) mentioned in the Canaanite Amarna letters (fourteenth century B.C.). The name itself means “flint.” Tyre was built on a large rock in the sea and was considered virtually impregnable until the fourth century B.C., when Alexander the Great conquered the city by building a causeway to it.

**delivered up a whole people.** See notes on v. 6.

**did not remember the covenant.** This phrase denotes the keeping of covenant obligations and is a standard phrase in ancient international covenants or treaties (cf. Gen. 9:15; Ex. 2:24; Lev. 26:42). Amos is asserting that Tyre did not keep its treaties with Israel.

**of brotherhood.** In the ancient Near East, kings entering into treaties styled themselves “brothers.” So Hiram of Tyre called Solomon “my brother” (1 Kin. 9:13; cf. 1 Kin. 5:12), as he had a background of treaty relations with David (2 Sam. 5:11). Later, Ahab continued the close relation with Phoenicia by marrying Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, the king of Sidon (1 Kin. 16:31).

verse_quote: pursued his brother with the sword.
note: See note on v. 6. This listing of events from the reign of Jehoram possibly includes Edom’s revolt and collusion with the Philistines and Arabs, who attacked Judah and entered Jerusalem, plundering the palace and deporting the royal household (2 Chr. 21:16, 17; Obad. 10–14).

Teman is a grandson of Esau (Gen. 36:11, 15). His descendant clan apparently gave its name to a region in the south of Edom, and to a village some fifteen miles (24 km) from Petra. Here, the region is meant. Teman was famous for wisdom (Job 2:11; Jer. 49:7).

**Bozrah.** The northernmost Edomite city, some thirty-five miles (56 km) north of Petra. By mentioning its northernmost and southernmost regions, Amos consigns all of Edom to destruction.

The Ammonites descended from Ben-ammi, the offspring of the trickery and incest of Lot’s younger daughter (Gen. 19:34–38). They lived between Aram and Moab.

**ripped open pregnant women.** This particular atrocity was practiced by others, including Hazael of Syria (2 Kin. 8:12), Menahem of Israel (2 Kin. 15:16), and Assyria (Hos. 13:16). The apparent purpose was to eliminate descendants who might try to reclaim the land.

**enlarge their border.** Ancient Near Eastern kings typically boasted that they extended the borders of their land. By doing so they fancied that they carried out the desire of their gods.

A short form of the fuller reference, “Rabbah of the Ammonites” (Deut. 3:11; 2 Sam. 12:26). This location is the modern Amman in Jordan near the spring that feeds the Jabbok River. The site is easily defended because it is surrounded by deep valleys and it has easy access to water sources.

**tempest ... whirlwind.** In Scripture, the figure of a violent and destructive storm is often used for the tumult of battle, as well as for the anger of God, or indeed for both at once (Pss. 83:15; Is. 5:28; 17:13; 29:6; 66:15; Jer. 4:13; 23:19; 25:32).

According to regular Assyrian practice, a conquered king, his household, and his officials were taken together into exile. Under Shalmaneser III (858–824 B.C.), Assyria conquered Ammon, making it an Assyrian vassal.

verse_quote: burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom.
note: According to Jewish tradition, these are the bones of the Moabite king Mesha. Such burning indicated special contempt and was thought to deprive the dead of peace in the afterlife. Josiah burned the bones of false priests on the altar at Bethel (2 Kin. 23:15, 16).

Probably the name of a major Moabite city and religious center (Jer. 48:41). The exact site is uncertain. Alternatively, the Hb. word might mean “towns,” as the Septuagint translators understood it.

**Moab shall die amid uproar.** The Hb. word used for “uproar” expresses a double entendre. It is associated both with the din of battle and with an archaic name for Moab, “the sons of tumult” (cf. Jer. 48:45).

**trumpet.** This is the ram’s horn (Hb. _shophar_), the signal horn of ancient warfare.
See note on 1:5.

The five oracles against pagan nations are concluded, and the southern kingdom of Judah is now addressed. Divine judgment moves ever closer to the northern kingdom of Israel, where Amos himself has prophesied (v. 6).

**rejected the law ... statutes.** For rejecting God’s revealed law, and so God Himself, they are particularly worthy of judgment (Deut. 4:39, 40). Judah’s covenant privileges imply greater responsibility (cf. Luke 12:48).

**after which their fathers walked.** “To walk after” is an idiom meaning to follow in obedience as a vassal or servant. Judah is following lies, and serving as the vassal of false gods or demons (Deut. 32:17; Rom. 6:16; 1 Cor. 10:20).

See note on 1:4.

**Jerusalem.** The name means “city of peace.” The Hb. word for “peace” (_shalom_) denotes not only the absence of war, but also the presence of prosperity and wholeness. Because Judah had not sought integrity in the Lord, she will see destruction, not peace. This prophecy is fulfilled more than 150 years later, when Nebuchadnezzar II conquers Jerusalem and burns every notable building, including the king’s palace (2 Kin. 25:8–10).

The indictment of the northern kingdom begins—Israel is guilty of social injustice, sexual immorality, and religious abuses (vv. 6–8).

**sell the righteous for silver.** A reference to the corrupt judicial system. Judges are willing to convict the innocent upon payment of a bribe.

**the needy.** The Lord has a special concern that their rights be protected (Ex. 23:6; Jer. 5:28), but they are being sold into slavery even for insignificant debts (here symbolized by a pair of sandals). Slavery in ancient Israel, though permitted in some forms, is carefully limited by the law of Moses (see Ex. 21:2; Deut. 15:12; 1 Pet. 2:18 and notes).

verse_quote: go in to the same girl.
note: Amos decries uncontrolled sexual passion. Such behavior is contrary to God’s original intention (Gen. 2:21–24; Matt. 19:4–6), and it profanes God’s holy name (Lev. 18:24). The Mosaic law prohibits sexual union among individuals closely related by blood (Lev. 18:6–18). While the Mosaic law does not mention this specific situation (the sharing of a common prostitute), the basic principle still applies. This is perhaps a reference to cultic prostitution; cf. v. 8.

They have engaged in fertility cult prostitution beside the altars, further profaning the Lord’s name. There are many altars in Israel, including those at Bethel (3:14), Dan (8:14), and Gilgal (Hos. 12:11). Their sins of sexual license and idolatry are compounded in that they have slept on clothing taken as pledges for loans to the poor. Such garments are not to be kept overnight (Ex. 22:26; Deut. 24:12, 13).

Faithful to His covenant promises (Gen. 15:16–21), the Lord drove out the Canaanites (simply called “the Amorite” here) from the Promised Land. See note on Gen. 10:16.

**like ... the cedars.** The description recalls the report of the twelve spies (Num. 13:32, 33), but also God’s wrath against all that is lofty and proud (Is. 2:12–18).

**fruit above ... roots beneath.** A poetic expression for complete destruction.

verse_quote: out of the land of Egypt.
note: By reminding them of His covenant faithfulness (cf. Gen. 50:24; Ex. 3:8), the Lord presses His case against Israel’s unfaithfulness.

The Lord sovereignly raises up prophets (Deut. 18:15–22), judges (Judg. 2:18), priests (1 Sam. 2:35), and kings (2 Sam. 7:12). The prophets serve as covenant lawsuit messengers, sent to recall the people to obedience.

**Nazirites.** See note on Num. 6:1–21. The OT mentions Samson by name as a Nazirite (Judg. 13:4, 5). Samuel was probably a Nazirite as well (1 Sam. 1:11 note). The three basic vows of the Nazirite are to abstain from consuming alcoholic drinks, touching dead bodies, and cutting one’s hair.

In contrast with the Lord’s faithfulness, Israel has sought to defeat God’s purposes by commanding His messengers not to prophesy, and by making the Nazirites drink wine (in violation of their vow). They have shown contempt for both the Lord and His law.
Just as a cart bogs down from the pressure of its contents and so becomes immovable, so Israel will be unable to flee (v. 14).
A vivid picture of helplessness: the fleet of foot will not escape, and the strong will not stand their ground.
All units of the army will fail before God’s anger.

Even the bravest warriors cast away not only armor and weapons but also every impediment, including clothing, in the panic of their useless flight. Such naked flight is an utter humiliation.

**in that day.** This phrase often indicates the Lord’s day of judgment (Zeph. 1:7 note). Here it refers to the approaching day of Assyrian conquest.

God prosecutes a lawsuit against Israel through His servant Amos (cf. Hos. 4:1–19).

**3:1 Hear this word.** This solemn command occurs again in 4:1 and 5:1, and echoes commands to hear and obey the Lord in the original covenantal documents (Deut. 4:1; 5:1; 6:3). It occurs regularly in covenant lawsuit material (Jer. 2:4; Hos. 4:1).

In addition to cognition (Gen. 4:9), the Hb. word for “know” has a wide range of meaning, including sexual relations (Gen. 4:1). Here the term denotes God’s sovereign choice, or election, of Israel as the object of His loving concern within a unique covenantal relationship (Ex. 19:4–6; cf. Deut. 7:7, 8).

**therefore.** The Lord’s gracious oversight of His people includes punishment for their sins precisely because He loves them too much to allow them to sin without discipline (Prov. 3:11, 12).

Amos presents a series of rhetorical questions, to which the answer in every case is quite clear. Their purpose is to emphasize that the message of Amos comes from the Lord.

**3:3 walk.** To “walk together” with someone here means to agree with his or her destination and route. Implicitly, the prophet “walks” with the Lord.
A silent hunter, the lion roars only after its victim’s fate is sealed. Just as there is reason for the lion’s roar, so also there must be a cause behind the prophet’s utterance.
No bird is caught in an unbaited trap.

See note on 2:2. Siege is a fearful prospect in Amos’s era, for it often results in starvation of the populace, followed by all the horrors of conquest: rape, pillage, slaughter, and burning.

**disaster.** Lit. “evil.” The OT teaches that the Lord is the creator of peace and of calamity (Is. 45:7). This does not mean that God is the author of evil, but rather that He sovereignly brings disaster or adversity on individuals and nations as just punishment. The curses pronounced in Gen. 3:14–19 show that the Lord brings such punishment.

The God who acts also reveals Himself and interprets His actions to and through the prophets. God revealed His plans for Sodom and Gomorrah to Abraham, the first “prophet” so designated in Scripture (Gen. 18:17; 20:7).

**his servants the prophets.** Moses, the supreme OT prophet, is called “the servant of the Lord” (Deut. 34:5). Subsequent prophets are characterized by the similar phrase, “my servants the prophets” (Jer. 7:25; Ezek. 38:17; cf. Dan. 9:10).
Just as a lion’s voice evokes fear, the voice of the Lord compels the prophets to proclaim His word (Deut. 18:18; cf. 1 Cor. 9:16).

The command is in the plural and apparently directed at the Lord’s servants the prophets.

**Ashdod ... Egypt.** Amos poetically summons the pagan nobility to look upon the injustice that reigns in Samaria. Israel (the northern kingdom) should have been more righteous, not less, than her pagan neighbors. It is ironic that these pagans should be called as witnesses to Israel’s misbehavior.

**mountains of Samaria.** Samaria is surrounded by mountains, from which the spectators are asked to view her.

**tumults.** Or, “disturbances,” as the word is translated in 2 Chr. 15:5. Such conditions result from sin and are the opposite of “peace” (Hb. _shalom_).
The ill-gotten gains from their violent and thieving behavior. The rich have plundered and looted the poor.
Assyria. The thought of this verse echoes the substance of the covenant curse for disobedience (Deut. 28:52).

According to ancient laws, shepherds are to demonstrate their diligence by rescuing a portion of a sheep taken by wild beasts (cf. Gen. 31:39 and note). The sheep of Israel will only be saved in a mutilated condition—in fact, the nation will be destroyed.

**with the corner of a couch.** The rich recline idly on couches (as the Romans later did at their banquets), enjoying the luxury they have extorted from the poor (6:4).

The command here (in the plural) may be to the pagans who have been summoned as witnesses, or to the Lord’s messengers, who are commanded to summon the pagan witnesses (v. 9 note). Or perhaps it is merely a general call to creation to be a witness to the broken covenant.

verse_quote: on the day ... for his transgressions.
note:
The phrasing here recalls the original covenant documents (Ex. 32:34).

**altars of Bethel.** This is one of the primary worship centers at the time of Amos. More than a century before Amos’s ministry, Jeroboam I made a golden calf for Israel to worship at Bethel in the north, as an alternative to worship at Jerusalem in the south, and installed an altar there (1 Kin. 12:25–33). Both altar and sanctuary were later destroyed by Josiah (2 Kin. 23:15).

**horns of the altar.** In Amos’s day, a fugitive can gain asylum by grasping the horns of the altar (1 Kin. 1:49–51), though the Israelites have been known not to observe this privilege (1 Kin. 2:28–35). Even this last resort for sinful Israel will be cut off.

The possession of both a summer and a winter house is a great luxury, affordable only by kings and the very wealthy. The Lord will destroy these multiple houses and decorated mansions. Assyria, God’s instrument of judgment (Is. 10:5, 6), is expert at such destruction and plunder, as the vast wealth of Nineveh during this period amply testifies (Nah. 2:9).

**houses of ivory.** Excavations at Samaria have uncovered a hoard of ivory pieces in the royal acropolis of the city. Most of them were found in the “ivory house” constructed by Ahab (see 1 Kin. 22:39). Many of the ivories are small plaques intended to adorn furniture, such as the “ivory beds” mentioned in Amos 6:4.

Through His servant Amos, God prosecutes a second covenant lawsuit against Israel.

**4:1 Hear this word.** See 3:1 and note.

**cows of Bashan.** The wealthy women of Samaria, who have been raised and cared for like the prime cattle of Bashan, a fertile area east of the Jordan River (Deut. 3:1 note) and northeast of the Sea of Galilee.

The same phrase occurs one other place in the OT (Ps. 89:35). No oath can be greater or more final (Heb. 6:13, 14).

**fishhooks.** The Assyrians of this period frequently lead prisoners by ropes attached to rings or hooks in their noses or lips.
This location is unknown.

These were important sites in the earlier history of Israel. Bethel was a sanctuary during the period of the judges, and Samuel judged both there and at Gilgal (1 Sam. 7:16). They became centers of syncretistic worship during the period of the divided kingdom (5:5).

**every three days.** Although the Hb. word for “day” can stand for a year or for an unspecified longer period (Gen. 1:5 note), three literal days seem to be meant here. Israel’s religious observances go even beyond what the law requires. Though enthusiastic about ritual, they have no living relationship with God.

The covenant law makes it clear that they are not to burn leavened bread as a sacrifice (Lev. 2:11; 6:17; 7:12). Amos sarcastically urges them to continue in their disobedience.

**for so you love.** In the ancient Near East, the term _to love_ had special significance in covenants: the vassal’s “love” for the sovereign entailed obedience (Deut. 6:5; cf. John 14:15). The nation’s disobedience has made it apparent to Amos that Israel loves rituals and idolatry rather than the Lord.

This section reviews what the Lord has done in punishment to warn His people and draw their attention back to Him. The emphatic phrase “I also” indicates the change of subject. All the disasters mentioned are threatened in the covenant document (Deut. 28). Israel should understand this and repent. But as the refrain repeats, “you did not return to me” (4:6, 8, 9, 10, 11).

**4:6 cleanness of teeth.** Their teeth are clean because they have nothing to eat. The covenant stipulations threaten hunger and want as a penalty for disobedience (Deut. 28:47, 48).

The winter rains from October through February are essential for the crops to begin their growth. The spring or “latter” rains of March and April will provide for mature growth (Jer. 5:24). The Lord promises these rains if Israel obeys His commands (Lev. 26:3, 4), but also warns that He will withhold them if they flagrantly and impenitently disobey Him (Lev. 26:18, 19; Deut. 28:23, 24).

**4:8 so two or three cities would wander to another city** . The Hb. verb translated “would wander” is used elsewhere to describe staggering movement associated with drunkenness. Desperately thirsty conditions are being depicted.

The Lord threatens these in the covenant document (Deut. 28:22; cf. Hag. 2:17).

**locust.** The Hb. word for this destructive insect probably derives from the verb meaning “to cut” (cf. Joel 1:4; 2:25). Ironically, the punishment described here is what the Lord had inflicted on Egypt (Ps. 105:34, 35), whose Pharaoh rebelled against God. Rebellious Israel has received the same punishment, and like Pharaoh has not repented.

The Lord had threatens a plague in His covenant with Israel (Deut. 28:21), along with all the diseases of Egypt (Deut. 28:60, 61).

**killed.** Yet another covenant curse fulfilled (Ex. 22:24).

Similar or identical phrases are used in prophecies against Babylon (Is. 13:19; Jer. 50:40) and Edom (Jer. 49:17, 18). The devastation of Sodom and Gomorrah provides a symbol of God’s judgment against sin (see Gen. 19:24, 25; Deut. 29:23 note). Here, God promises to overthrow Israel with equal thoroughness.

**a brand plucked out of the burning.** Despite God’s repeated mercy to His people (e.g., 2 Kin. 13:3–5; cf. Zech. 3:2), they remain ungrateful and unrepentant.

The phrase echoes Ex. 19:15–17, where, after three days of sanctification, the people met the Lord at Sinai. Then they met a God who was graciously forging a covenant with them. Now they will meet a God who is coming to judge their covenant disobedience.

This verse is in the form of an ancient Near Eastern divine or royal title: a series of titles or epithets used to describe the deeds or powers of a god or king. Here they describe the great King, who is abundantly able to carry out the curses He originally threatened in the covenant (cf. Is. 44:24–28).

**the L** ord**, the God of hosts.** See note on Zech. 1:3.

. This literary section is made up of many short prophetic oracles.

**5:1 Hear this word.** See 3:1 and note.

**lamentation.** As though in mourning for the dead, Amos pours out a lament for Israel. This literary device is frequently used in OT prophecy (e.g., Jer. 7:29; Ezek. 19:1; 26:17; 27:2; 32:2).

This term is used in other laments (e.g., 2 Sam. 1:19, 25, 27; 3:34; Lam. 2:21). Amos later uses the word to describe the “fallen” booth or house of David (9:11).

**virgin Israel.** This kind of personification is used of Israel (cf. Jer. 18:13; 2 Kin. 19:21) and of other nations such as Babylon (Is. 47:1) and Egypt (Jer. 46:11).
The drastic military reversals described here perhaps echo the prophecy of such disasters in the covenant that are the punishment for flagrant, impenitent idolatry (Deut. 32:15–18, 28–30).

This is a passionate plea for repentance and a call to turn back to God. The Lord has promised to meet those who would seek Him, even in exile (Deut. 4:29; cf. Lam. 3:25). Tragically, the Lord’s people often do not seek Him (Is. 9:13; Jer. 10:21).

See note on 4:4.

**Beersheba.** This ancient city (Gen. 21:31–33; 26:23–25; 46:1–5) is located fifty miles (80 km) south-southwest of Jerusalem, and is apparently a destination for religious pilgrims from the north in Amos’s day (8:14). Later, in the seventh century B.C., Josiah destroys the high places “from Geba to Beersheba” during his reform (2 Kin. 23:8). Excavations have revealed an Israelite temple here that was used from the ninth century onward. The temple has a structure similar to the temple in Jerusalem. It appears to have been created by the Israelites as a center for worship, but that temple is nowhere sanctioned by God’s law.

**Gilgal ... exile.** The words form an alliterative wordplay in Hebrew.

See note on 1:4.

**house of Joseph.** Ephraim and Manasseh, the tribes descending from Joseph (Gen. 48:15 note), whose tribal areas contain Bethel (Ephraim) and Gilgal (Manasseh), both mentioned in v. 5. These northern sanctuaries will be destroyed. Beersheba, in the south, will escape the fire of judgment that will sweep through the northern kingdom.

**none to quench it.** The Lord’s judgment fire cannot be extinguished (Is. 1:31; Jer. 4:4; Matt. 3:12).

These often occur together in the OT as qualities of life the Lord desires (v. 24; Is. 5:7).

**wormwood.** An herb found in Eurasia and North Africa that is poisonous in its pure oil state.

See note on 4:13. This majestic description of the Lord contrasts starkly with the previous verse.

**Pleiades.** A star cluster in the constellation Taurus that features six or seven prominent stars visible to the unaided eye. In many ancient Near Eastern cultures, the stars were thought to be personifications of deities.

**Orion.** In classical mythology, the constellation Orion is “the Hunter.” In Job also, the Pleiades and Orion are named together as evidences of God’s incomparable power and wisdom (Job 9:9; 38:31).

This verse contrasts with vv. 11, 12, which are in the second person. Such shifts of person are common in ancient Near Eastern writings of all kinds, and no significant difference of tone seems intended here.

**who reproves ... who speaks the truth.** A reference to those who reprove falsehood in court and bear true witness there. Israel has come to hate such men, presumably because they threaten practices of corruption and dishonest gain (2:6 and note).

**in the gate.** Much of a city’s legal business in this era is transacted in its gate, a large passageway with adjoining rooms. Excavations at Iron Age cities such as Gezer and Megiddo have uncovered benches inside the gateways; this is where the elders of the city sat and deliberated (cf. Ruth 4:1, 2).

These are costly to build, in contrast to the mud brick houses in which many people live (cf. Is. 9:10).

**you shall not dwell ... you shall not drink.** The curse of futility (failure to enjoy the fruit of one’s labor) fell on the Canaanites as Israel dispossessed them from their cities (Deut. 6:10, 11). Now Israel will suffer the same fate, according to the words of Deut. 28:30 (cf. Is. 65:21–23; 1 Cor. 15:58).

Israel needs to realize that the Lord knows what they seem to imagine that He does not know (cf. Ps. 73:11; Job 22:13, 14).

**bribe.** The Hb. term can refer to a common bribe (1 Sam. 12:3) or to a ransom for loss of life (Ex. 21:30).
This phrase explains why the prudent will be silent: the times will be so bad that the truth will not be tolerated.

For this thought of effective repentance, see Is. 1:16, 17. In 5:4 they were commanded to “Seek me,” for only God is good (Matt. 19:17).

**that you may live.** Obedience to the Lord will bring them security and prosperity (Deut. 28:1–14); but the verse points to a deeper truth, that to know God is life itself (John 17:3).

**God ... with you.** This is the deepest need of God’s people, expressed prophetically in the name _Immanuel_ (“God is with us,” Is. 7:14; cf. Matt. 1:23).

**as you have said.** Israel complacently claims that the Lord is with them, despite their rebelliousness, simply because He has made a covenant with them (cf. Matt. 3:9).

See note on v. 10.

**remnant of Joseph.** The northern kingdom of Israel is dominated by the tribe of Ephraim, descendants of one of Joseph’s sons (Deut. 33:17 note). Though Israel is relatively prosperous and strong, the phrase anticipates the future, after God’s judgment, when He will graciously restore a remnant of the people.
This possibly refers to professional mourners, who were common in the ancient Near East.

The laments over Israel will be taken up in every part of the land, since every part will be punished.

**I will pass through.** The same verb appears in Ex. 12:12, where the Lord speaks of His impending judgment on Egypt. Ironically, because Israel has become as pagan as Egypt, He must now “pass through” Israel in judgment as well (7:2 note).

This second portion of ch. 5 discusses the day of the Lord and His rejection of Israel.

**5:18 the day of the** LORD**.** Ultimately, this is the great and terrible “day of the Lord” when He comes in judgment (cf. Is. 2:12; 13:6–13; Obad. 15; Zeph. 1:7, 14). Every OT judgment is also a “day of the Lord,” and anticipates that final day. Joel describes it as a day of terrible judgment and destruction (Joel 1:15–20; 2:11). This time of judgment contrasts sharply with the redemptive outpouring of God’s Spirit (Joel 2:28–32).

**darkness, and not light.** The Lord alone has power to make day as dark as night, both literally and figuratively, in judgment (v. 8).
Amos vividly portrays the futility of trying to escape the Lord’s judgment (Is. 24:17, 18).

In addition to denoting physical light, the Hb. word for “brightness” is associated with the Lord (Ps. 18:12; Is. 4:5) and with the righteous (Prov. 4:18, 19; Is. 60:3; 62:1). There will be no light of righteousness in the land, and no brightness from the Lord’s favorable countenance. Judgment will be black and total, engulfing the whole land.

For a similar condemnation of empty ritual and sacrifice without repentance, see Mic. 6:6–8 (cf. Matt. 5:23, 24; 1 Cor. 13:3).

**5:21 I hate, I despise.** Two Hb. words here combine to express the attitude more forcefully than either could by itself. The result can be translated, “I reject with utter hatred.”

**I take no delight.** The language refers to burnt offerings. In the Mosaic covenant, the Lord declares that if His people are disobedient and unrepentant, He will “not smell” the fragrance of their offerings (Lev. 26:31).

verse_quote: Take away from me the noise of your songs.
note: The word for “noise” has a wide semantic range in Hebrew, but here it communicates a loud clamor or din (cf. 1 Sam. 14:19; 1 Kin. 18:41). The songs of the people are a loud disturbance, not pleasing to the Lord.

See note on v. 7.

**ever-flowing stream.** The streams, or wadis, of the Middle East are rocky watercourses through which torrents rush in the rainy season, but which are dry at other times. The Lord desires righteousness that is like His own—dependable, strong, and constant.

Offerings were brought to the Lord during the wilderness wanderings (Ex. 18:12; Lev. 9:8–24). The question emphasizes that such offerings were not of primary importance to the Lord then, and they are not of primary importance in Amos’s time either. Rather, He wants worship in spirit and in truth accompanied by true repentance.

Sikkuth (or Sakkuth) is an Assyrian deity associated with the planet Saturn. Kiyyun (or Kaiwan) is a Babylonian term for Saturn. Amos here refers to idols associated with astral deities that are carried in cultic processions. The Septuagint translates the Hebrew for “Sikkuth your king” as “tabernacle of Moloch” (the Hb. letters are similar), a reading quoted by Stephen in Acts 7:43.

**that you made for yourselves.** OT attacks on idolatry often focus on the merely man-made nature of the idols (Is. 44:9–20; Jer. 10:1–5; Mic. 5:13).
Banishment beyond Damascus in Syria implies exile to Assyria, as the prophet’s audience well understands. Exile far from home is the worst of the original covenant curses (Deut. 28:36, 64).

Zion (Jerusalem) and Samaria are the capitals of Judah and Israel, respectively. Like his contemporaries Hosea, Isaiah, and Micah, Amos is given prophecies that address both the southern and northern kingdoms (Is. 9:8–10:4; Hos. 6:4–11; Mic. 1:5).

**first of the nations.** The same ironic Hb. phrase occurs in Num. 24:20 (referring to Amalek). Israel has become powerful and prosperous under Jeroboam II, and might fancy herself the first among the nations.

The identity of this city is uncertain, but it may be the Calno mentioned in Is. 10:9, which was conquered by Sargon II of Assyria in 710 B.C.

**Hamath the great.** Located north of Dan on the Orontes River in Syria, it was restored to Israelite control by Jeroboam II (2 Kin. 14:23–25).

**Gath.** One of the five major Philistine cities (1:6 note), Judah’s Uzziah recaptured Gath from Syrian control (2 Kin. 12:17; 2 Chr. 26:6).

**Are you better ... is their territory greater.** The precise historical context and meaning of this verse is debated. Some suggest that Calneh, Hamath, and Gath have been conquered at the time of this prophecy, and that Israel should therefore not expect to escape conquest either. Others contend that Amos mentions other flourishing capitals of the region to show that Israel is as great as they, perhaps implying that Israel’s territory is not so small that aggressors will ignore it and attack these other cities instead.
Israel has enthroned violence, such as extortion and abuse of the poor, as a way of life, while also denying that the day of judgment is coming.

A symbol of wealth and luxury (3:15; 1 Kin. 10:22).

**calves ... stall.** Choice calves are kept in stalls and fattened for special occasions. Such is the normal fare for the wealthy of Samaria.
An ironic comparison with David’s musical interests. Unlike the Israelites, who pursue frivolous musical endeavors, David composed many psalms to the glory of the Lord (2 Sam. 23:1).

That is, from large bowls or basins. The same Hb. word is used for the large bowls before the altar at the temple (Num. 7:13; Zech. 14:20). The prophet’s hyperbole vividly portrays the excesses of the city.

**Joseph.** See note on 5:6.

verse_quote: first of those who go into exile.
note: This phrase is a Hb. wordplay on the earlier phrase, “first of the nations” (v. 1). Israel fancies herself the first among the nations, but will find herself leading the exiles.

A series of judgment pronouncements follow the indictments of vv. 1–7.

**6:8 sworn by himself.** Similar to oaths in Gen. 22:16; Ex. 32:13; Is. 45:23, here indicating that the judicial sentence is unalterable (Heb. 6:13 note). The Lord has no higher authority to swear by than Himself.

**pride of Jacob.** This refers both to Israel’s pride and to the very thing in which they have taken pride—their military strength. The word translated “strongholds” has the sense of “fortified palace” or “citadel.”
The meaning seems to be that small remnants hoping to escape will be found and killed.

Lit. “a man’s kinsman and his burner,” probably one and the same individual. Fear of epidemics may require cremation instead of burial in this era. Or, the burning could be a fire in honor of the dead (Jer. 34:5).

**must not mention the name of the** LORD**.** Previously, one might mention or invoke the Lord’s name for help, since He is the God of Israel’s covenant. But on the day of judgment one may not do this because the God of the covenant is coming in judgment (cf. Is. 48:1).

“Behold” frequently introduces noteworthy events. Here it signals the pronouncement that the Lord is rousing Assyria, His instrument of judgment, to come against Israel (cf. Is. 10:5, 6).

**great house ... little house.** Both the great houses of the wealthy and the small houses of the poor will be shattered by the coming judgment. This is a figure of speech called a merism, in which two opposites are all-inclusive: its use here demonstrates a total judgment. Here, as it often does in Hebrew, the word for “house” can also mean “household” or “family.”

Obviously not; no one runs a horse on such treacherous footing. Neither will one plow on rocks. But Israel’s injustice is just as absurd. A suggested reading of the second question, “Does one plow there with oxen,” requires a different word division in the Hebrew and is attested by no ancient version. It is better to take “rocks” as understood, although not explicitly stated, in the second query.

Lo-debar is a border town in Gilead, Karnaim a city on the plain of Bashan on the way to Damascus. They are both on the east side of the Jordan River. Both were apparently retaken from Hazael by Jehoash (2 Kin. 10:32, 33; 13:25), but later conquered by Assyria (2 Kin. 15:29). Respectively, the names mean “nothing” and “horns.” A wordplay is intended, by which Amos says that Israel rejoices in the conquest of nothing (the conquest of Lo-debar, soon to be taken by Assyria, is short-lived), and boasts of having taken “horns” (symbolic of military strength in the ancient Near East) by their own strength. Their conquests amount to nothing, and their strength will melt away before the Lord’s judgment.

Assyria.

**Lebo-hamath ... Brook of the Arabah.** The northern and southern boundaries of the kingdom as restored by Jeroboam II (2 Kin. 14:25).

This long section contains four visions (7:1–3; 7:4–6; 7:7–9; 8:1–3) and an autobiographical section related to the third vision (7:10–17). The first two visions have the following structure: (1) the Lord gives the vision; (2) Amos intercedes; (3) the Lord relents. Conversation between the Lord and His prophet is an integral part of the visionary experience.

**7:1 locusts.** This Hb. word, occurring only here and in Nah. 3:17, denotes swarming locusts just hatched.

**latter growth ... king’s mowings.** This verse seems to indicate that the first crop (the “king’s mowings”) represents the king’s share (cf. 5:11; 1 Kin. 12:4), while the farmer and his family depend on the second harvest for survival. Destruction of this second crop by locusts places the population at risk of starvation.

verse_quote: eating the grass of the land.
note:
The Hb. word for “grass” is general; all vegetation is destroyed, not just crops. In Hebrew, the whole phrase echoes the description of the locust plague in Ex. 10:12, 15 (“every plant in the land”). The Lord will punish Israel just as He punished Egypt before the exodus.

**please forgive.** Amos mediates and then pleads for God to show compassion on Israel.

Moved by intercessory appeal, the Lord is willing to relent concerning an intended punishment (cf. Ex. 32:12, 14; Joel 2:13; Jon. 3:10; Jer. 18:8). See note on Gen. 6:6. He has sworn that He will relent if the people repent.

See note on 1:4; Is. 66:15, 16.

**great deep ... land.** The “great deep” could be the Mediterranean Sea, although the same phrase is also used of the chaotic subterranean waters (Gen. 7:11 note), and of the Red Sea at Israel’s crossing (Is. 51:10). The prospect of a fire that will devour sea and land echoes the covenant judgment warning in Deut. 32:22. The language exceeds what happened in the OT, but foreshadows the last judgment (cf. 2 Pet. 3:10; Rev. 21:1), of which all previous judgments are but types.

This and the fourth vision (8:1–3) have the same structure: (1) the Lord gives the vision; (2) the Lord questions Amos; (3) Amos replies; (4) the Lord explains and judges. Similarly structured visionary experiences are recorded at Jer. 1:11–16.

**a wall built with a plumb line.** Most interpret this image to portray Israel as being judged in order to see if the people up to God’s standard. Others, following another analysis of the words (the word translated “plumb” resembles the Akkadian, or Assyrian, word for “tin”), render this “a wall of tin.” The same “wall” symbolism in Egyptian literature stands for military capability (cf. “wall of bronze,” Jer. 15:20; and “iron wall,” Ezek. 4:3). If this second interpretation is correct, the use of an Akkadian word for the metal indicates the source of the military power that the Lord will use to judge Israel.

**with a plumb line in his hand.** See note above. Many interpret this phrase as a reference to God’s covenant law, His standard of judgment. Others render this phrase “with tin in his hand,” a probable reference to Assyrian power, anticipating that He will put “tin” (i.e., Assyrian power) in the midst of His people (v. 8).
No longer will the Lord pass over their transgressions (Mic. 7:18).

These high places are traditional sites of pagan Canaanite worship (Deut. 12:2; 2 Kin. 17:10–12). The sanctuaries are for idolatrous or syncretistic worship. The appearance of these pagan worship centers in Israel demonstrates that the people did not meet God’s standards.

**house of Jeroboam ... sword.** Jeroboam himself might not die by the sword, but his household or family will be affected. Apparently, Jeroboam later died a natural death (2 Kin. 14:29), his son Zechariah was murdered (2 Kin. 15:10).

This autobiographical section apparently relates to the third vision, telling the reaction of Amaziah to the prophecies of Amos.

**7:10 the priest of Bethel.** Amaziah is probably the chief priest at the shrine of Bethel, and a representative of the priestly status quo.

**Amos has conspired.** The political implications of the prophet’s preaching are apparent. Jeremiah, too, was wrongly considered a traitor because of his prophecies against Judah (Jer. 26:11; 37:11–13; 38:1–6).

verse_quote: Jeroboam shall die by the sword.
note: Probably an allusion to the prophecy in v. 9. Amaziah misquotes Amos so as to make Jeroboam feel more personally threatened.

Probably this means “earn your living by prophesying there in Judah.” Although it is appropriate for a prophet to be paid for his work (1 Sam. 9:6–8; but cf. Mic. 3:5, 11), Amaziah accuses Amos of being merely a prophet for hire. Amaziah’s commands here are an example of the sin of commanding the prophets not to prophesy (2:12).

verse_quote: king’s sanctuary ... temple of the kingdom.
note: From the time when Jeroboam I established idolatry at Bethel (3:14 note) the kings of Israel have had a major influence on the cult. Amaziah is concerned for the sanctuary of his earthly king rather than for the sanctuary of the great King, the Lord. Ironically, Amaziah as the religious official is concerned only about protecting his earthly interests—and he charges Amos with conspiring against those interests (v. 10). A future generation of priests likewise puts to death Jesus, the greatest of the prophets, out of a wrong concern to protect their own kingdom and temple (John 11:48).

Unlike other prophets, Amos’s original vocation was not the prophetic ministry, nor is he one of the so-called sons of the prophets (i.e., disciples of the prophets; 1 Kin. 20:35; 2 Kin. 2:3, 5, 7, 15). He is not a paid professional prophet. Amos may also be signifying that he is performing this function by the election and call of God.

**herdsman.** See note on 1:1.

**dresser of sycamore figs.** One who treats the fruit by appropriate cutting to ensure superior sweetness once the fruit is ripe. Amos is skilled in more than one trade (1:1 note).

verse_quote: the LORD took me ... my people Israel.
note: Amos flatly rejects Amaziah’s accusation (7:12) and stresses his divine call to prophesy. The same phrasing is used for the Lord’s choice of David as king (2 Sam. 7:8). The prophet’s allusion to David’s call indicates that the Lord has the sovereign right to choose both kings and prophets—and that His prophets have every right to prophesy at the “temple of the kingdom” (v. 13).
See 2:12 and note; 7:12, 13.

Either by being ravished at the fall of the city, or out of desperation after the loss of family and wealth (cf. Deut. 28:30).

**your sons and your daughters.** Sons and daughters are often punished along with parents for covenant transgressions (Deut. 28:32, 53; Jer. 5:17; Ezek. 24:21). Violent death is a typical covenant punishment (Is. 3:25; Jer. 39:18).

**die in a unclean land.** Exile will be especially distasteful for the priest Amaziah: by living in a pagan land, he will become ritually unclean. See note on Lev. 11–16.

**Israel ... land.** Amos sarcastically quotes Amaziah’s own words from v. 11 back to him.

The Hb. words for “summer fruit” and “end” are similar, and are skillfully brought together here for effect. The vision of summer fruit indicates that the “end has come” for Israel. In addition, the appearance of summer fruit also denotes the end of the harvest period.

**never again pass by them.** See note on 7:8.

The Lord will no longer tolerate the noise of the temple songs (5:23), which will turn to the wailing of bereavement when the Lord comes in judgment.

**that day.** See note on 5:18.

**many dead bodies.** An abundance of corpses is typical in defeated cities in the ancient Near East, especially when conquered by the Assyrians (Nah. 3:3).
God charges Israel with social injustice, commercial dishonesty, and indifference to holy days.

The New Moon festival is celebrated every fourth week, with various offerings (Num. 28:11–15). The Sabbath, observed every week, is founded on God’s acts of creation (Ex. 20:8–11) and redemption (Deut. 5:12 note). Work is forbidden on these days.

**ephah small ... balances.** Such dishonest business practices are against the Lord’s law, and will result in His judgment (Lev. 19:36; Deut. 25:14).

See notes on 2:6.

**chaff of the wheat.** Lit. “the refuse of the wheat.” By mixing the chaff with the actual kernels of wheat, the estate owners cheat the buyers of their grain. These owners add to the good wheat that which falls the floor and is supposed to be discarded in the wheat threshing process.

This phrase may refer to the Lord Himself, or to the land of Israel, which is elsewhere called “our heritage ... the pride of Jacob” (Ps. 47:4). The oath in this verse dramatically introduces the forthcoming punishments. See note on 6:8.

Each year the Nile rises and overflows its banks, flooding the countryside and leaving rich deposits of silt. The imagery is used here to depict a coming flood of judgment—the upheaval of the Assyrian invasion (cf. Is. 8:7, 8).

See note on 5:18.

**I will make ... darken.** Though such idolatry is strictly prohibited by the covenant (Deut. 4:19), Judah and Israel have engaged in star and sun worship (5:26 note; 2 Kin. 23:5, 11). The assertions here affirm that the Lord alone is God, and the sun is merely one of His creations (Gen. 1:16 and notes).

**the earth.** Or, “the land,” since the land of Israel is to be punished. The phrase directly recalls the plague of darkness that the Lord brought upon the land of Egypt (cf. Ex. 10:21, 22; Ps. 105:28). Here again, the Lord is about to judge Israel in a manner similar to His judgment of Egypt.

This coarse material is worn as a sign of mourning to indicate that the pleasures of life no longer matter to the mourner (Gen. 37:34; 2 Sam. 3:31).

**baldness on every head.** Shaving the head is a sign of mourning. It is prohibited in the Sinai cov­enant (Lev. 21:5; Deut. 14:1), perhaps because it is a pagan practice of bodily disfigurement that disgraces God’s image (Is. 15:2, 3; Ezek. 27:30, 31). Ironically, it is prophesied for Israel and Judah (cf. Is. 3:24; Mic. 1:16).

**bitter.** A term describing the ultimate consequences of sin (2 Sam. 2:26; Prov. 5:4).

verse_quote: a famine ... of hearing the words.
note: This curse stems from the covenant law (Deut. 32:20; Hos. 3:4). So also in the period of the judges, when sin abounded (Judg. 21:25), “the word of the Lord was rare” (1 Sam. 3:1).
A standard phrase in the ancient Near East denoting “the ends of the earth,” this lit. means “from the Mediterranean to the Persian Gulf.”

Even the young and robust will be at the end of their strength (cf. Is. 51:20).

**thirst.** The focus is on physical extremity (cf. 4:7, 8), though spiritual thirst may be in view as well (v. 11).

This is likely a play on words: the Hb. word for “guilt” sounds like the name of the Canaanite goddess Asherah, the consort of Baal. To swear by a god in the ancient Near East of Amos’s day implies the recognition and worship of that god. Israelites are commanded to swear only by the Lord (Deut. 6:13; 10:20; cf. Jer. 5:7; Zeph. 1:5).

In the other four visions, Amos was an intercessor or respondent to the Lord’s questions (7:1–8:3 note; 7:7 note). In this vision, however, Amos has no active role but simply records what he sees.

**9:1 Strike the capitals.** That is, of the pillars. The command seems to be for an angel (cf. 2 Sam. 24:16; 2 Kin. 19:35) to destroy the temple by striking its pillars, bringing their capitals down on the heads of those within (cf. Judg. 16:29, 30).

Although the people may think that they can escape judgment, they will not find refuge from God’s pursuit.

**9:2 Sheol ... heaven.** This pair poetically expresses the comprehensive nature of God’s dominion (Ps. 139:7–12; Is. 7:11).

See 1:2 and note.

**bottom of the sea.** In contrast with the height of Mount Carmel. Since Carmel is on the coast of Israel, further flight will lead one into the sea.

**serpent.** This sea monster is perhaps the Leviathan of Is. 27:1. These lines of poetry assert the Lord’s sovereignty over all creation; none can escape His justice.
One of the covenant curses for disobedience (Deut. 28:41).

This section constitutes a short divine title (4:13 note), identifying the Lord as judge.

**9:5 touches ... melts.** For similar expressions of the Lord’s awesome power, see Ps. 46:6; 104:32; Nah. 1:5.

**rises ... sinks.** See note on 8:8.

**9:6 upper chambers.** This can be rendered “palace” or “temple” (cf. Rev. 11:19). The Hb. word means “steps” or “stairs,” such as those used to enter the temple, particularly the temple of the end time (Ezek. 40:6, 22, 26, 31, 34).

**vault.** Here it perhaps means the arch or vault of heaven (Ex. 24:10 note).

**the LORD is his name.** An exact repetition of the phrase in 5:8.

Lit. “like the sons of the Ethiopians,” the dark-skinned tribes south of Egypt (Gen. 10:6). Sinful Israel has rejected the covenant and is no more privileged than the Ethiopians, who are in a far land and do not reside where God has chosen to make His name dwell, namely, the Promised Land.

**Egypt ... Caphtor ... Kir.** By making Israel’s exodus from Egypt poetically parallel (and hence implicitly equal) to His dealings with other nations, God tells Israel that she has become no better than the pagans.

**Caphtor.** Crete.

**Syrians from Kir.** See note on 1:5.

Israel.

**not utterly destroy.** A graciously chosen remnant will survive.

The Lord will scatter His people among the nations, first by means of Assyria, which often resettles conquered peoples in different parts of its empire.

**as one shakes.** Figuratively separating the wheat (the faithful) from the chaff (the sinners), the experience of exile will serve to purify the nation of Israel (v. 10).
Denial of judgment, like denial of guilt, is characteristic of sin.

Amos concludes with an oracle of promised restoration ordered as follows: (1) reconstruction (v. 11); (2) conquest (v. 12); (3) fruitful abundance (v. 13); (4) rebuilding and replanting (v. 14); (5) enduring security (v. 15). Amos assures his readers that once the judgment of exile is past, restoration is as certain as was dispersion.

**9:11 In that day.** Possibly “the day of the Lord.” It is here depicted as the time of Israel’s deliverance (Zeph. 1:7 note).

**booth.** The “booth” represents the dynasty of David that, to the eyes of the prophet, is as good as fallen. But the tabernacle of David will be rebuilt. In Jesus, the greater Son of David, the dynasty of David has been reestablished (Matt. 1:1; Acts 15:16, 17).

Though subject to divine judgment (1:11, 12), a remnant of Edom will be brought under the redemptive kingship of David’s Son. Edom, and indeed all the nations, will benefit from coming under the dominion of this future King (Ps. 2:8). In Acts 15:16, 17, James applies this passage to God’s taking a people for Himself from among the Gentiles and including them in the church.

**and all the nations.** The addition of this phrase points to the fulfillment of the covenantal promise to Abraham that he would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4, 5).

**who are called by my name.** This phrase tells us that some, not all, from every Gentile group will come under the dominion of David’s Son. Only those who bear God’s name among all the nations will be included. The phrase (lit. “upon whom My name is called”) indicates subordination to His name and sometimes is used of Israel’s subordination to God’s covenant lordship (Deut. 28:10; Jer. 14:9). Amos foresees that the Lord will take possession of the remnant of all nations and will reign over them in a covenantal relationship through His messianic King (Acts 15:13–17).

A prediction of abundance, indeed more than abundance, follows the prophecies of disaster and desolation. The culmination of the Lord’s redemptive work through David’s greatest son, the Messiah, is portrayed in terms of endless cycles of fruitfulness that are reminiscent of Eden but surpass it (cf. Joel 3:18).

Lit. “turn the captivity of my people,” a recurring phrase in the prophetic covenant lawsuits (Jer. 29:14; Ezek. 16:53; Hos. 6:11).

**rebuild ... inhabit ... plant ... drink.** These blessings reverse the earlier futility curses (see 5:11 and note).

The Lord promises lasting safety for His people. God’s covenant with David promises an eternal kingship (v. 11; 2 Sam. 7:10). David’s greatest son, Jesus Christ, will guarantee redeemed Israel’s permanent blessedness.

**the land that I have given them.** See note on Gen. 13:15. The phrasing harks back to God’s cov­enant with Abraham and his descendants (Gen. 12:1, 7; 13:14–17; 15:18; 17:8). The physical Promised Land is but a type of the New Israel’s life in Christ; it points forward to the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb. 11:13–16; 12:22–24) and eternal inheritance (1 Pet. 1:3–5). The covenant land promise finds final fulfillment in the new heavens and the new earth (Rev. 21:1–22:6).
